intent: Eight individual shopping tasks preserve worth, bill/receipt timing, bus change, both required budget items, affordability scope, repairable-item conditions and profit after costs.
picturePurpose: Original hypothetical hilltop view supports the worth/effort context without pretending to prove price or duration. Exact sequence and budget inclusion remain coded.

transfer.stem: Which plan preserves the payment order, receipt timing and budget items?
transfer.passage:
Planning what to keep and pay
A visitor said the hilltop view was worth the long climb. This valued the effort; it did not put a price on the view. Before buying supplies, we checked the bill before paying. We kept the receipt until we had tested a new lamp. That instruction did not mean throwing the receipt away before the test or requiring immediate disposal afterwards.
Our budget had to cover paint and brushes, so both items needed to be included. No amounts were supplied. We asked whether we had enough change for the bus without assuming we already did. We could not afford a new printer this term, which did not mean we could never buy one.
We avoided wasting money replacing repairable things, without making a rule against every replacement. A stall made a small profit on each notebook: profit was distinct from the full amount received before costs, and the number sold was not given.

options.text: Check the bill after paying; keep the receipt until testing; budget for both paint and brushes.
Check the bill before paying; discard the receipt before testing; budget for both paint and brushes.
Check the bill before paying; keep the receipt until testing; budget for paint but omit brushes.
Check the bill before paying; keep the receipt until testing; budget for both paint and brushes.

answer.display: Check the bill before paying; keep the receipt until testing; budget for both paint and brushes.
